terms.def: An attached house sharing side walls (party walls) with its neighbors in a continuous row.
terms.spot: Identical or related facades in an unbroken line along the block.

terms.def: In New York usage, any single-family (or small multi-family) house in the city, row or freestanding; originally a rich family's city residence.
terms.spot: Real estate shorthand, often for a wider or grander house.

terms.def: New York shorthand for almost any 19th-century rowhouse, whether faced in brownstone, brick or limestone.
terms.spot: If someone calls a red-brick Greek Revival house a brownstone, they're using it this way.

terms.def: A single wall shared by two adjoining buildings, usually straddling the property line, with each owner having rights in it. Work on it can affect the neighbor, so it often needs their consent.
terms.spot: The side walls of a rowhouse. Ask what's shared before structural work.

terms.def: An apartment that occupies an entire floor of a rowhouse, with windows front and back.
terms.spot: Front and rear exposures in one unit.
ex: Brownstone rentals in Brooklyn and Harlem

terms.def: An apartment whose rooms are lined up one behind the next, with no hallway. Bedrooms are usually pass-through rooms, which matters for roommates and privacy.
terms.spot: You walk through each room to reach the next, like train cars.
ex: Tenements in the East Village and Greenpoint

terms.def: Walk-up apartment buildings built under the Tenement House Act of 1879, many with a "dumbbell" plan pinched in the middle for an airshaft. Expect small rooms, some with little light, and no elevator.
terms.spot: Five or six stories, narrow lot, front fire escape; interior rooms lit by a tiny shaft.
ex: Five- and six-story walk-ups on the Lower East Side and in the East Village built 1879–1901
The Tenement Museum, 97 Orchard St, is the earlier pre-law type (1863), built before any light or air rules

terms.def: Apartment buildings built after the Tenement House Act of 1901, which required larger courts, windows in every room and indoor toilets.
terms.spot: Wider buildings, often on two or more lots, with real courtyards.
ex: Walk-ups in Washington Heights and the South Bronx

terms.def: An open court cut into a building's footprint to bring light and air to inner rooms.
terms.spot: A U, H or E-shaped building plan with an open notch facing the street or rear.
ex: Prewar apartment buildings along Riverside Drive
terms.q: light court apartment building Riverside Drive

terms.def: A narrow vertical shaft between or within buildings, meant to ventilate interior rooms.
terms.spot: Windows facing a brick wall a few feet away.
ex: Old-law tenements on the Lower East Side

terms.def: The first respectable middle-class apartment houses, from the 1870s, borrowed from Paris to overcome the stigma of tenement living.
terms.spot: 1870s–1880s apartment buildings, usually five or six stories with modest ornament and stores at the base; they look like tenements but have larger windows and grander entrances.
ex: Stuyvesant Apartments, East 18th St (1870, Richard Morris Hunt; demolished)

terms.def: A building of suites without full kitchens, served by a central kitchen and hotel staff. Most have since become ordinary co-ops, condos or rentals, and some units' kitchens were added later and can be small.
terms.spot: Grand early-1900s buildings; many units now have converted kitchens.

terms.def: Built before World War II, typically 1900–1940, prized for thick walls, high ceilings and gracious layouts. Many are co-ops, so expect board approval and rules on financing and renovations; plumbing and wiring may be original.
terms.spot: Plaster walls, 9–11 foot ceilings, formal entry gallery, separate dining room, solid hardwood floors.
ex: Classic co-ops on West End Ave and Park Ave

terms.def: Built after World War II, roughly 1945–1980, usually with lower ceilings and more open layouts than prewar.
terms.spot: 8-foot ceilings, balconies, through-wall air conditioning sleeves, simple lobbies.
ex: East Side towers along Second and Third Avenues

terms.def: Postwar planning that set apartment towers in open lawns and plazas instead of along the street.
terms.spot: Repeated towers on a superblock with no through streets.

terms.def: Low-rise apartment buildings grouped around shared interior gardens.
terms.spot: Four- to six-story buildings wrapping a private landscaped block interior.

terms.def: A former stable for horses and carriages, often now a house.
terms.spot: Wide arched ground-floor openings where carriage doors were; hayloft doors above.

terms.def: A small lane of former stables and carriage houses behind grand houses.
terms.spot: A gated, cobbled lane of low buildings.

terms.def: A former factory or warehouse floor with high ceilings, big windows and open space, converted to homes. In SoHo and NoHo many lofts were legally limited to certified artists, so check the certificate of occupancy.
terms.spot: Columns in the middle of the room, 12-foot-plus ceilings, oversized windows, freight elevator.

terms.def: Originally a small structure on a roof; now the top-floor apartment, often with terraces on the setbacks.
terms.spot: Top-floor units, often set back from the facade with terraces. In listings, "PH" may just mean the top floor, so don't assume outdoor space.
ex: Setback terraces of Central Park West towers

terms.def: The broad lower base of a tower, often lining the street, from which a slimmer tower rises.
terms.spot: A block of a few stories filling the lot, then a narrower tower above.

terms.def: A skyscraper at least 300 meters (about 984 feet) tall.
terms.spot: Billionaires' Row along 57th Street is the densest cluster.

terms.def: An extremely slender tower, very tall relative to its narrow base.
terms.spot: Roughly 10:1 or more height to width. 111 West 57th is about 24:1.

terms.def: A tall, narrow building on a small midblock lot, restricted by the 1983 sliver law in many residential districts.
terms.spot: A tower squeezed between low buildings on a lot 45 feet wide or less.
ex: Narrow 1970s–80s towers on Upper East Side side streets

terms.def: Unused development rights above a property that can be sold to a neighboring lot, letting the neighbor build taller. For a buyer, a low building next door with unused rights can mean a future tower and a lost view.
terms.spot: A tower rising over a low landmark next door often bought that landmark's air rights.
ex: Towers around Grand Central using the terminal's transferred rights

terms.def: A building or district protected by the Landmarks Preservation Commission, created in 1965 after the loss of Penn Station. Owners need LPC approval for exterior work, including windows and rooftop additions, which adds time and cost.
terms.spot: Look up the address on the LPC's map; plaques are not a reliable sign. Within a historic district, every building is covered, even plain ones.
ex: Brooklyn Heights, the city's first historic district (1965)
